parameters.name: table
parameters.description: The table to filter. Usually a physical table name or ALL(Table) to ignore existing filters.
parameters.examNote: Using ALL(Table) as the first argument ignores existing filters — common when used inside CALCULATE.

parameters.name: filter_expression
parameters.description: A condition evaluated for every row. Rows where this evaluates to TRUE are kept.
parameters.examNote: This runs in row context — it can reference the current row's column values directly.

returnType: Table (a filtered subset of the input table)
summary: FILTER returns a table containing only rows that satisfy a condition. Unlike simple boolean filter arguments in CALCULATE, FILTER can express complex multi-column conditions and is itself an iterator.

examples.label: Filter to high-value transactions
examples.explanation: FILTER keeps only rows where Amount > 300 (Bike: 400, Gloves: 350). CALCULATE sums those: 400 + 350 = 750.

steps: FILTER iterates every row of the input table
The filter_expression is evaluated in each row's context (row context)
Rows where the expression evaluates to TRUE are retained
A new filtered table is returned — not a scalar

commonTraps: FILTER returns a TABLE, not a scalar — it cannot be used alone as a measure. Wrap it inside CALCULATE, COUNTROWS, or another table function.
Prefer simple boolean filter arguments in CALCULATE for single-column conditions — FILTER adds overhead and is needed only for multi-column or complex conditions.
FILTER(Table, ...) respects the current filter context; FILTER(ALL(Table), ...) ignores it — choose carefully.
